#1052. Graham Potter on his Swedish love affair, Viktor Gyokeres and World Cup pain: ‘You’re in this amazing bubble and then it’s gone’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Sweden manager Graham Potter tells Lawrence Ostlere about the ‘strange’ emptiness of World Cup elimination, lessons of tournament football and the challenge of building a team to compete with Europe’s best

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

What does it feel like to be knocked out of the World Cup? For weeks you’re inside your own fraternity, a brotherhood going into battle every few days. Then you lose 3-0 to France and it all stops. Cancel the hotels and the flights. No more games, no more training sessions, no more team meetings. One manager recently described the desolation of defeat, wallowing alone in their hotel room as players and staff left for the nearest airport.

“It’s a good description of it,” nods Graham Potter, whose Sweden side were beaten by France this summer in the round of 32. “There’s a week or so where you’re in a bit of an empty state. It’s nothing that I’ve experienced before. For weeks you’re in this amazing bubble where you eat, sleep, drink, work, everything together with these people, and then it’s gone. You don’t know whether that group of people are going to be together again.”

Sweden did have one last evening before they went their separate ways, and they just so happened to be a short ride from Manhattan. “We were in a hotel in New Jersey, so we managed to find our way into New York and had a dinner and a few drinks with the staff, and just enjoyed one night together. And then everybody’s away, and it feels very strange.”

Once the dust had settled, Potter gathered his assistants and analysts to pore over Sweden’s tournament in detail – “a fun part of the job,” he says. Some joined on Zoom calls from their club roles while others met at the Swedish FA headquarters in Stockholm, including the former Sunderland midfielder Seb Larsson, who can often be seen in Potter’s ear. “I haven’t played international football and certainly not for Sweden, and he’s played 130 games, so his experience and understanding of the national team is fantastic,” Potter says.

There were mixed feelings. The World Cup had started perfectly, with a 5-1 win over Tunisia. But a 5-1 defeat by Netherlands and a 1-1 draw with Japan left Sweden third in the group, sending them into the path of the all-powerful French, and they were played off the pitch in New Jersey.

“It’s never nice to lose but sometimes you have to go, ‘OK, maybe the better team won’. But then you have to go, ‘how could we have played better?’ Those thoughts aren’t necessarily in detail on that evening [in Manhattan] but that’s certainly where your brain goes quickly. You have to zoom out and go, ‘OK, we’re disappointed now and it feels really s**t. But would we have taken this when we came in?’ Yeah, of course.”

Potter is meeting The Independent in London in the midst of an impressive Nations League campaign, with Sweden on the verge of promotion to the top tier. He is enjoying the wild ride that has been his first international job, in charge of his adopted country. Potter says he feels Swedish and he sings the national anthem with West Midlands gusto.

It is an unlikely love affair which began when the 35-year-old Potter, who had just graduated from Leeds Metropolitan University with a master’s degree in leadership, took a job no one else wanted in the remote city of Ostersund. The Potters arrived in the depths of winter, when enormous piles of snow line the roads and the sun shines for barely five hours. His wife cried every day for months.

“She’d left her job, her life. It wasn’t like moving to Monaco, especially when you arrive in January, when it’s minus 20-something outside and dark by two o’clock in the afternoon. It’s a wonderful place, but it was tough initially. It’s the fourth tier of Swedish football. So there are times where you’re going, ‘OK, is this right for life and family?’ But you have to give it that time, and thankfully we stuck together and stuck it out, and it was the best thing we’ve ever done. It was worth it.”

After 15 years of highs and lows in the club game, Potter took charge of Sweden last October following a disastrous World Cup qualifying campaign under predecessor Jon Dahl Tomasson. Sweden had one last shot at salvation through the play-offs in March.

He quickly learnt two things about the rhythms of international football. The first is time: enormous gaps of time, yawning canyons of time, almost too much of it. Potter, who owns a house in Sweden but still lives near Brighton, spent the four-month wait for the play-offs flying around Europe meeting his new players. He’d be in the centre of Dortmund one day and the medieval streets of Bergamo the next, then on to London, Liverpool, Newcastle and Glasgow.

“My passport was crammed because you’re just having a half-hour, 40-minute coffee and conversation with players. It’s nice to get a sense of where their careers are at, where their family are at, how they see the situation, because I came into a bad situation. I found it’s very useful to build a relationship, and then it’s very useful to have an understanding of what they’re doing in their clubs.”

Then, suddenly there’s no time at all. The players flew into Valencia for the play-offs on Monday, and on Thursday they played Ukraine in a semi-final. “We had a day and a half [to prepare] and it’s a play-off to go to the World Cup,” Potter says. “So is the game going to be about intricate passes from the back and nice patterns of attacking play? We needed to win two matches. So our starting point was defensive stability, strong in set-pieces and counter-attacking, because we had big-space players like Viktor Gyokeres and Anthony Elanga who are as good as anybody in the world attacking big areas.”

Gyokeres scored a hat-trick to beat Ukraine and then smashed home a dramatic, last-gasp winner to beat Poland and send Sweden to the World Cup, where Potter learnt something else: the brutal finality of tournament football, that shock at a journey ending in the middle.

He spoke to players individually over the summer and found a consensus: they relished the World Cup but left desperate to compete with teams as strong as Netherlands and France. There were signs of life against the Dutch, despite the lopsided scoreline, when Potter changed to a more attacking formation in the first hydration break and Sweden dominated until half-time. The French game, however, was utterly one-sided.

“How do we get to the point where we can beat France? The reality is, if you’re Sweden, you have to have Alex Isak firing off the back of a good season, and probably he wasn’t at that stage. You need Dejan Kulusevski, one of your best players. Isak Hien wasn’t available, our first-choice centre-back. So you want to arrive with the very best that you have.

“The players that we have, when you look at Gyokeres and Isak and Kulusevski and [Yasin] Ayari and [Lucas] Bergvall, there’s a certain profile to them that you have to set up to be proactive against whoever you face, and that’s probably the disappointing thing or the learning point – we weren’t able to do that against France, and if you’re going to lose a game, you’d rather lose in the way we played against the Dutch than how we did against France, even though the scoreline is still painful.

“The players are at a point where they want that type of football. They want to play proactively, they want to play positively, and that’s the exciting challenge.”

There have been signs of evolving into a front-foot team in Sweden’s impressive start to the Nations League, after winning three games and drawing one to take control of Group H with Bosnia, Poland and Romania. Another win over Bosnia on Saturday will seal promotion to League A with Europe’s heavyweights.

Gyokeres has led the charge, scoring in all four Nations League games to take his Sweden record under Potter to 10 goals in 11 matches. He has featured only intermittently for Arsenal this season, but Potter isn’t concerned.

“It doesn’t really matter, is the truth, because he’s done brilliant for us when he’s been playing every week [for Arsenal], and he’s done brilliant for us when he hasn’t been playing every week. Whatever he does in his club, that’s part of the thing that you can’t control. You just have to accept that, and then you just make sure that from a loading perspective, when he comes in you’re careful with him. But he’s such a professional, fit guy that loves playing football for Sweden.”

Kulusevski missed the World Cup through injury but made his long-awaited return to the Tottenham team last month, and Potter sent him a text ahead of the game. “It was just a beautiful moment to see him on the pitch. I’ve not worked with him, that's how long he’s been away, but everybody in the national team says he’s so important, so influential.”

While Kulusevski has been absent, his future brother-in-law has become essential. Yasin Ayari, who is engaged to Kulusevski’s sister Sandra, has been at the heart of Brighton’s flying start to the season and his form for Sweden has been outstanding, with two goals at the World Cup and a starring role in recent Nations League games. “His improvement, I would say from November last year, has been incredible,” beams Potter.

The task now, with Euro 2028 ahead, is to turn Sweden’s most talented group for a generation into a side who can go toe-to-toe with the best teams in the world, to give themselves every chance of staying a little longer before the music stops.

“We all shared the same thing, which was that the World Cup was an amazing experience. But we want to keep going, we want to evolve, we want to improve. It’s not like we’re happy with what we did. We’ve done a lot of good things. The atmosphere in the group was fantastic, amazing, so we took some important steps. But at the same time, you want it to go on. We weren’t ready to go home.”

The former Liverpool man insists he won’t be adding to the ranks of ex-pros on the primetime BBC show

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For two decades, Danny Murphy enjoyed a hugely successful playing career, winning a host of major honours with Liverpool and earning nine England caps.

Since hanging up his boots in 2013, the former Crewe Alexandra academy graduate has become a familiar face in the media, making regular appearances for the BBC on television and radio.

And while Murphy has found his groove as a pundit, there are some broadcasting avenues that he has no desire to go down.

Ratings-behemoth Strictly Come Dancing is one of the BBC’s most popular shows and has seen plenty of sports stars swap the playing field for the ballroom in recent years.

Former Lionesses star Karen Carney became the first ex-footballer to claim the glitterball last year, while Shaun Wright-Phillips bowed out five weeks into the current series.

But any fans wanting to see Murphy swap the commentary box for the sequins and become the latest ex-player to strut his stuff on the dancefloor will be left disappointed.

“I’ve turned Strictly down twice,” Murphy tells FourFourTwo. “I enjoy a good dance, but I’m not into sequins and I’ve got a busy life – it had nothing to do with money.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For some sporting personalities, appearing on Strictly has been a way to show off a different side of themselves, but Murphy is content to leave this particular challenge to others.

Instead, the ex-Fulham and Tottenham man simply knows where his interests lie and does not feel the need to step out of his comfort zone and into the Strictly limelight.

“For me, the less limelight, the better,” he continues. “I love talking about football, it’s the one area in life that I feel I know something about.”

This preference for sticking to his strengths is why Murphy rejects the idea of taking on an entirely new challenge in front of millions of viewers.

“Crossing over to do something that isn’t my strong point? It’s not for me,” he concludes.

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1050. The summer that changed Welsh football

"Walking to the ground in Bordeaux and what I find hilarious, in hindsight, is how low our expectations were."

Wales had gone more than half a century without playing at a major tournament, so it was understandable that expectations were modest.

Generations of fans had been scarred by agonising near misses and downright dismal failures of the past so, when Wales finally realised a nation's dream by qualifying for Euro 2016, just being there was enough for many.

Bordeaux was bathed in sunshine on the afternoon of Saturday, 11 June, tens of thousands of Welsh supporters descending on the French city for their opening game against Slovakia.

"We were all saying things like, 'Oh, the anthem's going to be good, that's guaranteed'. We could have lost 10-0 but they were definitely playing the anthem," the comedian and presenter tells BBC Sport Wales as part of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football.

An anthem heard at a major tournament for the first time in 58 years. Glorious catharsis to stir the soul.

Wales had ridden a wave of emotion to get there, a golden generation of players - Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey et al - scaling new heights under the guidance of their charismatic manager Chris Coleman.

"I was saying to all the players, 'Keep calm, don't act like we're too excited to be here'," Coleman recalls.

"But Bordeaux was like the centre of Cardiff, Welsh fans everywhere outside the hotel and, as soon as we were getting on the bus, I was chanting with the fans! I was like, 'What am I doing? Calm down'. I got lost in it."

Coleman and his players eventually composed themselves. After a trademark Bale free-kick had put Wales in front, Hal Robson-Kanu came off the bench to score a late winner and send a nation into raptures.

"Euro 2016 was a turning point for Welsh football," says Ben Davies, the Tottenham Hotspur defender who made a crucial goalline block early in the game.

"There was so much talk about 1958 and I'd heard about it, I'd seen the odd clip about it, but it felt like a pipedream to actually have Wales in a major tournament.

"So to do it, forget about how well we did in it, just to even get to that tournament, it gave us a belief that it was possible."

For those among the sea of red shirts in Bordeaux that day, it did not feel like life could get any better - but this was only the beginning.

This was the summer that would change Welsh football forever.

âIt was like being in the centre of Cardiff â there were Welsh fans everywhereâ

Until Euro 2016, Wales' story had been dominated by tales of heartache, Joe Jordan's handball in 1977 and the Romania defeat of 1993 among many painful chapters.

But by getting to France, Wales freed themselves from that history.

"There had been some really low points for Wales, so to finally do that was a huge achievement," says Ramsey, the then Arsenal midfielder who would go on to be named in Uefa's team of the tournament.

Wales had momentum they had never felt before coming into the competition. Victory over Slovakia - and the prospect of getting to the second round - took that to another level.

A last-gasp defeat by England in Lens momentarily punctured that optimism, but the final group game against Russia presented Coleman's side with a chance to secure their place in the knockout stages.

This was meant to be nerve-wracking for a team with no major tournament experience against seasoned opponents.

But under a lilac sunset in Toulouse, Coleman's men played with a flair and verve unlike any other Wales side.

"That was our best performance," says Coleman. "We were awesome."

Wales cut Russia to ribbons with a breathtaking attacking display, racing into a 2-0 lead in 20 minutes.

After Ramsey's delicate finish put Wales in front, they poured forward with such gusto that even Neil Taylor scored - the wing-back's first goal since he was playing in non-league for Wrexham six years earlier.

"When Tayls scored, that summed up how things were falling for us," says Joe Allen, who was exceptional in midfield that night.

"This was one of those once-in-a-lifetime moments you've got to capitalise on."

That is exactly what Wales did. Bale added a third in the second half to become the tournament's top scorer at that point, and the winning margin could have been even wider.

Joe Ledley (right) dances in front of the Wales fans after the 3-0 win over Russia in Toulouse

"We completely dominated them," says Joe Ledley, who ran the game alongside Allen in midfield.

As well as Ledley played, though, what elevated him to cult status was his post-match dancing in front of the Wales fans.

"I don't know where those moves came from," he grins. "I used to dance with my mates all the time at local pubs in Fairwater [in Cardiff]. I just went for it."

Wales fans could scarcely believe what they had witnessed. Having already lived a dreamlike existence in France, this was starting to feel surreal.

The odyssey took them to Paris next, Wales' first knockout fixture since Pele had scored the only goal as Brazil beat them in a 1958 World Cup quarter-final.

This time, Coleman's men had the novelty of being favourites against an obdurate Northern Ireland side, who made life difficult for their opponents in a tense last-16 tie.

Bale eventually prised them open â his cross turned into his own net by Gareth McAuley â to set up a quarter-final against Belgium, and what would turn out to be the greatest night in Welsh football history.

'I remember like it was yesterday' - Euro 2016 hero Robson-Kanu

Wales fans made a lasting impression in France, with their distinctive bucket hats and chant of 'Don't Take Me Home', which became an unofficial anthem of the Euros. Uefa even gave them an "outstanding contribution" award.

"What I loved about Welsh supporters at the Euros was we were just desperate to enjoy every second and suck the marrow out of it because we didn't know if it was going to happen again," says James.

"We're there to have fun. I'm not saying the result was secondary, but we all had realistic expectations."

No wonder when you consider Wales' quarter-final opponents were Belgium, ranked number one in the world at the time with a squad boasting stellar talents such as Kevin de Bruyne, Romelu Lukaku and Eden Hazard.

"That Belgian side, on paper, was like a team to represent Earth against Mars," James adds. "It was like a team from space."

It did not help matters that the game was essentially a home fixture for Belgium, whose fans filled the stadium in Lille, fewer than 10 miles from the Belgian border.

The odds were stacked against Coleman and his players, lengthening further when Radja Nainggolan's thunderous long-range strike gave Belgium an early lead.

But Wales believed they could win, not least because they had beaten Belgium in a qualifier in Cardiff 13 months earlier, and they responded magnificently as captain Ashley Williams headed in a deserved equaliser.

Then, nine minutes into the second half, Bale played a raking long ball to Ramsey, who found Robson-Kanu in the penalty area. And time stood still.

"I remember controlling the ball in the box and there was momentum carrying everyone away from the goal," Robson-Kanu says. "I just remember Cruyffing the entire opposition."

With a manoeuvre as audacious as it was inspired, Robson-Kanu flummoxed three surrounding Belgian defenders with a Cruyff-turn before finishing supremely beyond Thibaut Courtois.

Wales' fans came to be known as the Red Wall during Euro 2016

"It was an out-of-body experience," adds the forward, who was without a club at the time.

"Looking back, you realise careers are defined by moments, and to have a moment that you're truly remembered for is a real honour."

Belgium pushed desperately for an equaliser but Sam Vokes headed in superbly to seal a 3-1 triumph. The celebrations were as ecstatic on the touchline as they were in the stands; disbelief as it dawned on players, staff and fans that Wales were heading to their first semi-final.

"There are certain moments in your life that are so good you wish you could just stop it and say, 'Let's just sit in this moment'," says Coleman.

"That was one of those moments. We got back in the dressing room and I can't describe the atmosphere."

Allen, another Welshman in Uefa's team of the tournament, adds: "That's the moment where it crossed from being a good story into, 'This is more than anyone dreamed was possible'."

The next, and what would prove to be the final, stop on Wales' magical ride was a semi-final against eventual champions Portugal in Lyon.

Shorn of the suspended Ramsey and Davies, Wales were stifled by their canny opponents, who secured a 2-0 win with second-half goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Nani.

This was the end of the adventure in France, but the beginning of a glorious era for Welsh football.

"It was a really important moment for Wales, our history and generations to come," says Ramsey.

Having been absent from major tournaments for 58 years, Wales went on to qualify for a second successive European Championship, before achieving what Davies describes as the "holy grail" of reaching a first World Cup for 64 years in 2022.

"We opened the door that had been closed a long time," says Coleman.

The milestones kept coming, with the women's side qualifying for their first major tournament at Euro 2025.

Whereas Welsh national teams only used to dream of playing on the world's grandest stages, there is now an expectation they get there â and that stems from 2016.

Wales players and staff celebrate with their fans after their Euro 2016 quarter-final win over Belgium

"With more money coming in from qualification for the European Championships, particularly Euro 2016, we ended up being more cash-rich," says Jonathan Ford, chief executive of the Football Association of Wales (FAW) from 2009 to 2021.

"That enabled us to put more money across the board: women's football, grassroots football. We transformed the women's game."

Uefa vice-president Laura McAllister is a former captain of Wales who played a leading role in getting the FAW to formally establish a national women's team in the 1990s.

"There was nothing inevitable about what happened post-2016 and that's why I think we should give credit to the FAW, and Jonathan Ford particularly, for steering us out of the tournament into that era," says McAllister.

"I was part of the FAW Trust in 2016. I can remember times before that when Jonathan came into the board and said things like, 'Until the men qualify for a major tournament, we can't invest in X, Y and Z'. And that included the women's national team.

"While I bristled at that because it felt unfair, the financial realities of the FAW meant until the men got to a position where they generated income from participating and winning, it was going to be impossible for us to deliver the strategy we had for Welsh football."

McAllister travelled to France 10 years ago as a fan, and Qatar in 2022 to cheer on Wales' men at a World Cup.

When the women played at Euro 2025 in Switzerland, McAllister was there again to see the legacy not only of her own pioneering work in establishing the team but the far-reaching effects of 2016.

"Something happens when you qualify. It's flicking a switch in mentality - it becomes something realistic and achievable," she adds.

"What matters far more is what you do with the breakthrough moment, not how you've performed."

Wales' women are now trying to take the next step of qualifying for their first World Cup, while the men looked on enviously as their showpiece event happened without them in the United States, Canada and Mexico this summer.

Disappointing as it was, that frustration itself represented a shift in mindset that came after Euro 2016 â a sharp contrast to the passive acceptance that met Wales' previous absence from major tournaments.

Since that golden month in France, Wales feel like they belong at this level.

"The best thing we could give the teams coming after us was to say it's possible," says Coleman.

Subsequent qualifications have been the legacy of Euro 2016, while future ambitions are proof of a desire to ensure generations to come continue to build on the foundations laid by their predecessors.

There is plenty more Wales' men and women want to achieve but, whatever happens, there will never be another summer quite like Euro 2016.

"We're so proud of each other and what we achieved," says Ledley.

"Nobody thought we'd do it. When I walk down the street now, everyone says, 'Thank you for 2016, the best summer of my life'."

James can attest to that. "It remains the best month of my life," he says. "I don't think you often know it's the best month of your life as it's happening."

With the benefit of hindsight, it is laughable to think you could find a Welsh football fan who would disagree.

You can listen to all three episodes of Iconic: The Summer that Changed Welsh Football on BBC Sounds.

Romeo Lavia completed his first Premier League 90 minutes in a Chelsea shirt against Michael Carrick’s Manchester United last weekend

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Chelsea bounced back from their disappointing home defeat to rivals Tottenham Hotspur with a solid 2-0 home triumph over Manchester United last weekend. Xabi Alonso has now overseen five wins and three defeats in his opening nine league matches. It’s been a topsy-turvy start to life in his debut campaign at Stamford Bridge.

It perhaps is no coincidence, then, that three of their five wins have come with Romeo Lavia in the starting XI. The Belgian started his fifth league match of the season in the victory last weekend. It marked the first time the 22-year-old has played the full 90 minutes in the Premier League game since his 2023 arrival from Southampton.

“It was a top-class performance. His performance was very complete from a midfielder’s point of view,” the Chelsea head coach said. From an individual as talented as Alonso was in his playing days, it was high praise indeed.

The issue for Lavia, though, has so often been the inability to remain fit for prolonged periods of time. Saturday marked just his 20th top-flight start since making the move to the capital. He’s already bettered last season’s haul of four league starts. Yet when fit, the former Saints man showcased just why he has had the faith of managers, both past and present.

Operating at the base of the 4-2-3-1 setup, Alonso needs a player who is able to both retain possession and advance play effectively. As he proved against Man United, Lavia does so to a very good standard. An 88.9% pass success rate was the fifth highest of all Chelsea starters in that game, while only Wesley Fofana (76) made more passes (72).

Only Morgan Rogers, Estevao and Cole Palmer (3 each) created more chances than Lavia's two, who was credited with the assist for the former’s opener. Admittedly, Rogers did all the hard work as he slalomed through the Man United midfield and finished with aplomb. Nevertheless, it was a commendable haul from Lavia, who prior to the win had created just two chances in the previous six league outings combined.

Admittedly, Lisandro Martinez’s dismissal midway through the second half helped the Blues' cause. That they were able to maximise their numerical advantage is testament to Chelsea’s in-game management under Alonso.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

It proved Lavia is more than just a tempo-setter in the middle of the park. After all, he finished top for tackles (5) and second for interceptions (4) of all Chelsea players last weekend. The youngster maintained a 100% tackle success rate in the home triumph.

Some might assume that Lavia and Moises Caicedo will compete for the same position in the team, but that would be a common misconception. Both carried out their own individual roles in the win over Michael Carrick’s men, as Caicedo fared slightly better in possession, which in turn enabled Chelsea to dominate proceedings.

Either way, it was a partnership that worked well together, and one that supporters surely hope provides the midfield foundation for the west London side going forward. That will only come to fruition, however, should Lavia completely overcome his injury issues. A lack of European action will aid the player, with lower demands on his body to play once every three days.

In the end, it was a stroke of luck that brought Lavia back into the fold. Read misfortune, if you’re Chelsea or summer transfer target Lamine Camara. The Blues agreed a fee with Monaco for the Senegal international, only for the French side to pull the plug on the deal at the last minute as striker Folarin Balogun closed in a switch to Everton. The American’s move fell through, and it meant Monaco were stuck with the pair, which, due to financial issues, was far from ideal.

Chelsea’s loss has since proven to be Lavia’s gain. Keeping him fit in the long-run is now the priority. Yet, with Alonso seemingly managing his workload accordingly, and praising him following the standout display against Man United, Chelsea’s failure to get the Camara deal over the line could, ultimately, prove their gain, too.

Lavia had become something of a forgotten man in Cobham, as he spent ample time in the physio room. Saturday proved a timely reminder of his quality and showed why, when available, he should be Caicedo’s midfield partner in Alonso’s favoured setup.

Ben is a freelance football expert with over 15 years of experience in the field, ranging from stats, to betting, to transfer analysis, to news, and everything in between. Having departed esteemed football stats website WhoScored.com in 2025, he has been touring the freelance circuit, and has been featured on The Guardian, The Independent, Sky Sports, The Premier League, TNT Sports, ESPN, Squawka and talkSPORT, among others.

#1047. How the Man City case could spark a drastic change in English football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Over a third of the league is now up for sale, writes Miguel Delaney, but despite the Man City case, this major shift could bring a solve one of English football’s major problems

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Over the past few weeks, those in Premier League boardrooms have noticed a very distinctive shift.

The previous talk of trying to buy clubs, only for billionaires to realise how few are available, has gradually turned into talk of trying to sell clubs.

The current calculation is that at least eight clubs - over a third of the league - are either officially or unofficially up for sale in some form.

With some of these, there are actual prospectuses. With others, it’s that an ownership would be open to listening to offers. Some would consider full sales, others merely minority stakes.

The current problem, though, is that there are so few buyers.

The market has changed, but it could offer the opportunity for a wider reset.

That may be dependent on a much bigger story, which is a factor in all of this, following the recent developments surrounding the Manchester City case.

Right now, it’s only a few months since another distinctive story - Jeff Bezos’ consortium buying a stake in Liverpool - seemed to mark a high point of high-level purchases.

The Premier League was at that moment seen as a good area to invest due to how it is uncorrelated to global markets, helping to diversify investment portfolios, and this on the back of a boom of US institutional money buying clubs after Covid.

Many of the same factors are now working in reverse.

The great takeover has become the great sell-off. Or, at least, attempted sell-off.

At “absolute level”, one source describes it to The Independent, no one is buying, and there has been “stagnation” in the market.

Some activity still persists at a fractional/minority level but only if it represents real “value”.

Part of it, one experienced source stresses, is “circumstantial”. No deals are going to get through the Independent Football Regulator this side of Christmas, so there is little movement.

Other industry figures stress that billionaires aren’t as willing to invest, due to ongoing global uncertainty. The one tendency is for such billionaires to invest within US sports. Arsenal’s owners, the Kroenke family, struck a deal to buy the Los Angeles Angels for $4bn in September, while Josh Kushner and Bog Iger pulled off a record-breaking $12.5bn deal for the Los Angeles Lakers in August.

The crisis in the Gulf, among other concerns, could affect flow of money in football given how much investment comes from that region. So many corners of the game are now indirectly dependent on it.

The rumours about Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund’s willingness to sell Newcastle United have been swirling for at least two years.

Perhaps most pertinently, though, many buyers see English football as being in an opposite situation to a half-decade ago.

Amid so many takeovers, it was viewed as “a growing trend”, which is generally seen as the best type of business for such investors to get into.

Now, most clubs do not have growing revenues. The English game is seen as having “topped out”.

That could be made clear in the next broadcasting rights cycle, since the last one in the Premier League saw the price per game drop for the first time in the competition’s history.

The current expectation is that domestic rights will stay around the same level and that international rights will marginally drop - unless there’s an unlikely entry from one of the streaming giants.

All of that only deepens the sense that “the Bs” of Brentford, Brighton and Bournemouth are excelling, since they all have superb operations and strategy departments.

Few other clubs have that scope for growth.

There’s then that other looming story: City.

A lot of people are waiting to see how that case concludes, especially since it could see the Abu Dhabi ownership sell up, too.

No matter what happens, the very nature of the City story is viewed as inevitably bringing some kind of reset.

Even in the most basic terms, a usually locked-in Champions League place may be opened, and that for a few years. Financial projections can be altered.

Should City unexpectedly prove successful in their appeal, though, they’re back in the centre of all of this and potentially emboldened.

Many prospective ownerships and investors want to see how this lands before acting.

Another layer is if this leads to a forced sale, and potentially a much bigger discussion about state or state-linked ownership.

If such purchases are restricted, it does change the market. Overall ceiling is lowered.

All of this runs alongside a deeper argument that the introduction of the Independent Football Regulator coming in conjunction with the City case offers a rare opportunity for a reset anyway. And not just a reset.

But, given how both developments have involved discussion about core principles of English football, a proper rethink about what the game actually wants to be; what clubs and owners should be; what their role is.

This very increased focus on executives and takeovers only makes clearer the climate we’re in.

English football has gone from the era of the player, up to 1945, through the era of the manager, up to 2003, into the era of the owner. That is to say, the figures that exert the greatest influence on the game.

As the clearest illustration of this, something has obviously gone wrong if a series of clubs with self-sustainably huge fanbases have entire eras completely defined by who their owners happen to be.

In a properly run game, football outlook would be independent of this.

Instead, you only have to look at the examples of Manchester United under the Glazers, Newcastle United under Mike Ashley and arguably his successors, Liverpool under Tom Hicks and George Gillett… and on and on.

The national sport really shouldn’t come down to the pot luck of which of the one per cent picks you, especially when the Independent Football Regulator has specifically recognised the social importance of the game as a matter of law.

That’s also precisely why any future financial regulations shouldn’t be dependent on owner investment, despite so much agitation.

One of the biggest problems in English football right now is a £300m per annum commercial revenue gap between the wealthiest clubs and the rest.

It has been made close to unbridgeable by a system that, as one source tells The Independent, ensures “a hole below the waterline in competitive balance”.

The wage inflation from that similarly drags football’s entire financial system upwards, forcing high-risk capital investment, and creating more and more stress.

That stress has in turn had the effect of ensuring a fan-owned club like AFC Wimbledon have to consider selling off stakes to private investment, despite the Independent Football Regulator expressly encouraging fan ownership.

The system the regulator oversees instead seems to work against that.

It should be a sign, to go with everything else. There has never been a better moment for a reset.

#1046. Life as a Wag in the transfer window

"Owen was on the phone to the manager and his agent while I was in labour. They waited for me to give birth and then he went out on loan pretty much as soon as I was out of hospital."

Owen Dale's loan deal wasn't to a local club, but to Portsmouth - a city more than 200 miles away. His partner, Jessica Beaumont, had never even been there.

And the pair had only just got the keys to a house they had bought. They would end up staying in it for just one night.

"Since living together, we've moved five times in five years," says Jessica.

"You have to be prepared for anything in the transfer window. But it's also a really fortunate position to be in at a young age."

This period - when clubs are permitted to buy, sell and loan players - takes place twice a year, in January and during the summer, for clubs in the Premier League, the English Football League (EFL) and the Women's Super League (WSL).

While a select few stay in one place throughout their career, for most players moving from club to club is just part of life in the modern game.

Jessica met Owen when he was at Crewe Alexandra. A move to Blackpool soon followed.

"I didn't get together with him because he was a footballer so I never considered the footballer life - that he might just have to move at the last minute," she says. "We just met and we clicked."

But it soon became apparent that dealing with almost constant uncertainty would be part of that life.

The move to Blackpool was a loan, with an option to buy, so for six months - during which Jessica was pregnant with their son Xavier - they did not know whether he would be staying there or heading back to Crewe.

Blackpool decided to sign Owen, but he was soon out on loan again. This isn't uncommon, with loan deals a way for clubs to help young prospects gain first-team experience and get regular playing time elsewhere.

"When the move to Portsmouth happened it really hit me - I had to quickly realise that 'OK this is now my life'," says Jessica.

Just before Owen's loan deal to Portsmouth the couple had bought their first house together in Congleton - a town close to Jessica's family in Stoke on Trent, and commutable to Blackpool.

"We spent one night in there - we hadn't even unpacked," she says.

They decided a 10-hour round trip on Owen's day off in the week to see his newborn son was not an option.

"We thought 'if he's not playing well because he's tired, what's the point in doing this'?" says Jessica, who adds that they ended up renting out the Congleton house and have been living in rented accommodation themselves ever since.

"I was finishing my law degree and had a job at the time - I had to say to them I wouldn't be coming back from maternity leave," she says.

Post-natal complications also made it difficult for her to travel at the time.

"I had Owen on the phone basically saying, 'I've done a couple of house viewings. I've chosen this one. This is where we're going to be living' and showing me on FaceTime," she recalls.

"In that moment I did feel really out of control."

Uprooting her life at short notice and leaving her family behind was challenging and Jessica remembers spending a lot of time alone in Portsmouth when Owen was at away games.

But she remembers lots of positives from that time too, including when she became friends with another player's partner.

"I was so fortunate that she would often stay with me when Owen was away," she says.

"I say to her all the time that I'll appreciate that time forever because I was just so isolated.

"Our schedules were the same - when Owen went away her partner was also away - I didn't have to be fully alone and she got it."

Owen made 28 appearances for Plymouth Argyle last season

Owen, now 27, has played most of his career in League One, with two stints in the Championship when we was with Blackpool and Oxford United.

Last season was spent on loan at Plymouth Argyle and he is currently a free agent - this means he is not tied to any club by a legal contract. Owen can now join a new team without a transfer fee because no former employer owns his registration rights.

Many of his moves have been on deadline day and he says he is "very aware of the sacrifices" his family make.

"There's always the risk that a move might not work," he says. "So I might uproot my whole family for this next venture and it all goes south.

"Over the years I've learned that until there's a contract signed on the dotted line, you could end up anywhere."

Owen went on loan to Portsmouth in 2022 just days after Jessica gave birth to Xavier

Owen returned to Blackpool the following year and made 32 appearances for the Tangerines

The family moved to Bicester in 2024, as Owen helped Oxford United win promotion to the Championship

Owen joined Wigan Athletic on loan the following year making his debut in a 2â1 FA Cup fourth-round defeat by Fulham

Last season the family lived in Devon after Owen went on loan again - this time to Plymouth Argyle

For now, Jessica's career in law is on hold, she instead has a job in social media and works from home.

She also posts about her experiences on TikTok, regularly using #wag and #waglife.

"My career can be picked up at any time - whereas his career is right now and you've really got to take every opportunity," she says.

"As much as people say it's a glamorous lifestyle you do make sacrifices so your partner can have their dream and get themselves as far as they can in football.

"At the end of the day, as much as I'm involved, it's his career. That means in order for me to support him properly I can't get emotionally involved."

This includes not getting too emotionally attached to where they live.

"We usually rent newer houses that are a blank canvas so we can make them our own, although this last season the accommodation was provided furnished by Argyle," she says.

"We put a lot of Xavier's toys and garden stuff in storage and referred to our Plymouth accommodation as 'the holiday house'.

"It can be hard when he asks us to get things like his trampoline which we don't have with us."

Owen's career is always the priority, Jessica says.

"When Owen was at Oxford he had one year left on his contract and I loved it there," she says.

"But the best thing was for him to go and get game time somewhere miles away. So we moved."

While Premier League footballers can earn tens of thousands of pounds a week - sometimes hundreds of thousands - life in the lower leagues can be very different.

"When you think 'Wag' [players' wives and girlfriends] and you think 'footballer', both of those terms come with this stereotype that our lives are easy," Jessica says.

"People also put League One players in the same bracket as Premier League players.

"In the Premier League they're often set up for life - we can't live in that way because we have to prepare for life after football."

Adding to the uncertainty of where they will be playing is also the possibility or relegation or injury.

"When we were at Portsmouth, Blackpool was still his parent club and they got relegated," says Jessica. "Owen wasn't even involved that season, but his wage was still affected.

"You have to be prepared for everything. You just can't live outside of your means.

"But it's still a really fortunate position to be in.

"Luckily, Owen's been good with injuries. There are some players who they get injured in the last month of the season and they're out of contract.

"In football things can be really positive or really negative."

The uncertainty also affects their children - four-year-old Xavier and two-month old Etta.

"Now that Xavier is growing up - he's fast approaching school age - another thing that will have to be added into the mix is his stability," says Jessica.

Even normal things like organising his recent fourth birthday party aren't always straightforward.

"We couldn't plan to have a party in Plymouth with balloons and cakes etc because we didn't know if we were going to be there," she says.

"Instead we planned a party near my family in Stoke-on-Trent - we needed to make something work regardless of what happens with Owen's job.

"As much as I worry about Xavier and Etta, I also think how amazing it's going to be for them when they're older to be able to tell their life story and say they've lived in all these different places.

"I think it's teaching them a good life lesson that they don't need to be tied to one place."

She says they have made every move a positive experience.

"We've said to Xavier that we might be moving soon and when we do we're going to get his bike back out of storage," says Jessica.

"That way he knows that moving is a possibility and hopefully he's not thinking about what he's going to lose but what he's going to gain.

"The fortunate thing for us is that Xavier loves football. He gets a lot of excitement as well from the new strips and the new chants and all of that kind of thing."

Xavier has enjoyed watching his dad play at each of his new clubs

So, does Jessica have any tips for people in a similar situation?

"The main thing for me personally - and what I've learned first hand - is the importance of keeping your own identity outside of football," she says.

"If you get too wrapped up in it, it only puts more pressure on your partner.

"If you can get a hobby, a routine or even a work-from-home job, that can help - things that can move with you."

Being sensible financially is also important.

"I'd also say that if you have a season where you get promoted, try not to change your lifestyle and to bank the promotion money so that you have as much stability as you can," she adds.

"In our house, I de-clutter maybe once a month," she says. "This helps me because I don't have control over Owen's career. But what I do have control over is making sure that if and when anything does happen, the house is ready to be packed up and moved.

"When it's the transfer window I will plan in one-week blocks - that gives me that little bit of certainty in a situation where I have no control."

She admits "it can be hard" but "on the flip side it's so exciting".

"We've lived in places that we never would have lived in. And that's exciting for a relationship," she adds.

"You know, with some relationships you can get bored.

#1045. From VAR to ticket prices, football needs fixing – here are 30 ways to make the game better
