Mauricio Pochettino has been linked with the soon-to-be vacant Manchester United position repeatedly for the best part of 10 years

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a revealing sit-down with FourFourTwo last year, USMNT head coach Mauricio Pochettino has finally lifted the lid on a legendary encounter with Sir Alex Ferguson, a meeting that has fuelled a decade of what-ifs at Old Trafford.

The Argentine, who took the reigns of the US national side on a contract running through until 2030, recounted how the most successful manager in British history once sought him out.

“Through the secretary of the League Managers Association, Sir Alex asked for my phone number so that we could have lunch," Pochettino told FourFourTwo.

"It was a meeting in London between colleagues, between a genius and an apprentice.”

The lunch, which took place some years ago during Pochettino’s tenure at Tottenham Hotspur, has long been cited as the moment Manchester United first identified him as their long-term successor.

Despite those historic links which persisted through his stints at Paris Saint-Germain and Chelsea, the stars never quite aligned for Pochettino to take the hot seat in Manchester.

The USMNT boss shared a charming anecdote from the afternoon that proved it's not just his footballing tactics that are up to scratch, it's trivia, too.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“When we asked for the bill, I wanted to take it, and so did he. We started arguing over who’d pay!

"He said, ‘Stop Mauricio, I’m going to ask you a question. If you answer correctly, you pay. If not, I’ll pay.’

"He said, ‘Name an Argentine player who scored in the 1930 World Cup final.’ I replied, ‘Stabile.’ He couldn’t believe it. The name came to me out of nowhere! In the end, I paid the bill.”

Despite his current focus, having led the USMNT at their home World Cup earlier this year, Pochettino has freely admitted he would like a return to the Premier League some day.

"Right now it’s about enjoying the World Cup," he said. "After that, I’ve always said I came so close to winning the Premier League and Champions League, and want to try again. I’d like to be part of a project with the ambition of winning both."

Pochettino’s comments are especially relevant as Man United face what looks to be another period of transition.

Michael Carrick is expected to be relieved of his duties at Old Trafford during November's international break. For now, the self-proclaimed 'apprentice' remains on the international stage, but the pull of a Premier League return is unmistakable.

Pochettino's USMNT take on Haiti in a Concacaf Nations League double header this month.

#971. Which Premier League players are set for yellow card suspensions?

Harry Maguire and Alexis Mac Allister are among 13 players on the brink of a one-match ban

The first one-match suspensions for yellow card offences in the 2026-27 Premier League season have now been served.

Hull City's Matt Crooks and Aston Villa's Matty Cash became the first players to receive a ban for accumulating five yellow cards before gameweek 19.

Players receive a one-match suspension if they pick up five or more yellow cards prior to the conclusion of their team's 19th league match of the season.

There are now 13 players sitting on four bookings after 10 rounds of matches, meaning they must avoid another yellow card prior to the halfway point of the season to avoid a ban.

Bournemouth have the most players on the brink of a ban, with three players one yellow card away from suspension.

After that date, the threshold increases to 10 yellow cards. Any player reaching that number before the end of their club's 32nd league match of the season will receive a two-match suspension.

From that point, there are further thresholds at 15 and 20 yellow cards.

For players reaching 15 cautions, they incur a three-match suspension. Punishments for players reaching 20 yellow cards are determined by a regulatory commission.

Those cut-offs do not reset until the end of the Premier League season.

In the Championship, League One and League Two, there are similar thresholds.

However, with those three divisions having 46 rounds of league matches instead of 38, players have to avoid getting 10 yellow cards before the end of the 37th league match in order to not receive a two-match suspension.

In those divisions, the yellow cards are reset at the end of the league season and do not include matches in the play-offs.

The following players have served a one-match ban and will now receive a two-match ban if they reach ten bookings before game week 32:

#970. England's best? Record-breaking Ballon d'Or winner Kane set for Wembley celebration

England captain Harry Kane set to win record-breaking 126th England cap in Nations League this week; Kane was voted England's greatest in a Sky Sports poll - but biggest prize still awaits; follow England vs Croatia with the Sky Sports website and app on Thursday; kick-off 7.45pm

Senior Football Journalist @psmithXI

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Harry Kane is set to become England's most-capped player ever on Thursday night - will it also be time to crown him the country's greatest?

Kane's Ballon d'Or triumph last month coronated him as the world's best for the past year. Whether he should have the all-time No 1 spot for his country makes for a fascinating debate - not least with the weight of a World Cup win on the side of historic icons such as Bobby Charlton (another Ballon d'Or winner) and Bobby Moore (another captain fantastic).

But, minus the big team triumph, Kane's individual case is compelling.

Interestingly, Sky Sports readers went for Kane when we asked the question following his 125th cap for the Three Lions in October. Kane took 49 per cent of the vote from almost 100,000 respondents.

A major-tournament win would surely take him into undisputed territory. Cruelly, through two European Championship finals - including one settled on penalties at Wembley - and two World Cup semi-final heartaches, that international trophy currently remains elusive.

After ending his club trophy wait with his move to Bayern Munich, Kane would dearly love the latter years of his career to also bring England success. Perhaps the Nations League is where he and his team-mates will break that long wait for silverware? England are almost certain of a place in March's quarter-finals and can make a statement against Croatia and Spain this week.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

But even without the big England win, Kane's huge goal haul, consistency, leadership and multi-faceted quality put him on a pedestal. He is guaranteed a fitting show of respect and admiration for all of that ahead of kick-off with Croatia.

Kane is almost certain to start that fixture, meaning he will go to 126 appearances for his country, one more than legendary goalkeeper Peter Shilton.

International games come more frequently these days, of course, but Kane's relentlessness is well worthy of celebration. He's always hungry to get onto the pitch and go for goals and that's reflected in his stats. He has been unavailable for just one of the past 101 competitive matches England have played, a defeat to Greece in 2024 in the Nations League.

Inevitably there have been highs and lows - and plenty of criticism to ride through before what is likely to be a night of tribute this week.

The agonising campaign to add to that World Cup win of Moore, Charlton and co goes on but in the Kane era, England have never gone closer. From going to the final four in 2018 in Russia to the painful turnaround loss to Argentina in the USA which ultimately led to a third-place World Cup finish, Kane has been a central figure.

There have been moments when he has been fiercely scrutinised, particularly in summers when it appeared he was worn out by the rigours of the previous season.

There have been big misses - from close range against Croatia in that World Cup semi-final, for instance, or his second penalty against France at the 2022 World Cup, when he skied the ball off target when he looked primed to take the quarter-final to extra-time.

But mainly there have been goals. So many goals. For years, Charlton's total of 49 was the record total for an England player. Wayne Rooney just managed to overhaul it at the end of his career, lifting the bar to 53. Kane has smashed it. He's up to 91 and counting, as prolific as he's ever been.

On the occasion of his 125th cap against the Czech Republic, he added two more to his total. A Croatia side who he also struck twice against in that incredible 7-0 victory in October will be fearing more punishment from the England skipper.

With a long-coveted Ballon d'Or in his possession, Kane appears to be at the peak of his powers: the goal machine who can also set up opportunities for others and make the play from deep. An all-round superstar.

On Thursday, those stratospheric heights he's reached will be recognised. But be sure, Kane - along with England supporters - will be wondering whether he and this team can go even higher for the truly magnificent prizes they all crave.

Follow England vs Croatia with the Sky Sports website and App on Thursday; kick-off 7.45pm

#969. Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:

double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

Meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”

Out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”

Blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he says he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he said.

The 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Manchester United look ready to appoint Mauricio Pochettino, with the former Tottenham Hotspur coach happy to accept.

Pochettino is currently enjoying life as manager of the United States men's national team manager, overseeing the 2026 World Cup hosts' journey to the quarter-finals on home soil over the summer.

With Manchester United lingering in the bottom three of the Premier League and Michael Carrick expected to be sacked now, the Argentine has emerged as the frontrunner for the job at Old Trafford.

According to David Ornstein of The Athletic, United are to sack Michael Carrick, despite the recent upturn in form.

United have picked up four points from the last two games, against Roma in the Champions League and Aston Villa in the Premier League – but in both fixtures, Carrick watched his side go two goals down before fighting back to salvage a result.

With Pochettino emerging as the favourite for the role now, TEAMtalk have revealed that he would “jump at the chance” to return to club football with the fallen giant.

The report adds that “there has been no direct contact between United and Pochettino, or his representatives, at this stage.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The Athletic have revealed that it would cost $10 million to relieve Pochettino from his contract with the USMNT – though free agent Eddie Howe also has a fee, with Newcastle United holding a compensation clause in his exit.

Pochettino has long been linked with a move to Old Trafford – as far back as his Tottenham days – with his name touted for the job regularly over the years.

The 54-year-old last managed in the English top flight with Chelsea in 2023/24, taking the Blues to a respectable sixth in the table, after the club had finished 12th and burned through three managers in BlueCo's first season in charge.

Carrick signed a contract in May to continue as United's head coach through to 2028, but has overseen an appalling start to the season, with the club 18th in the league and 17th in the league phase of the Champions League.

The Red Devils have one a single league game all season, the fewest in the English top tier.

Manchester United travel away to Liverpool when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#967. Mongolia’s iconic grasslands are in crisis — invisible fungi could help save them

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

April Reese is a journalist in Aveiro, Portugal.

More than 70% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, which has implications for the country’s nomadic herders.Credit: Timothy Allen/Getty

Rising temperatures, desertification and overgrazing are taking a heavy toll on Mongolia’s iconic desert grasslands, as well as its nomadic herding culture. But a team of researchers might have hit on an underground solution. They’ve found clues that protecting key fungal networks that support life above the surface could help to preserve biodiversity, boost climate resilience and revive degraded lands.

In most ecosystems, invisible networks of fungi trade resources with plants by interlocking with their roots. These arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi provide the plants with nitrogen and phosphorus gathered from the soil; in return, the plants send excess carbon through their roots to the fungi, helping to sequester it from the atmosphere.

“Mongolia has very unique fungal networks that power these arid grasslands,” says evolutionary biologist Toby Kiers at the Free University of Amsterdam. Kiers is leading a project to map and identify mycorrhizal-fungus hotspots in Mongolia. “As we fight desertification, we want to be able to protect the fungi that are going to be so important for these plants and ecosystems to be restored.”

Working out ways to maintain healthy fungal networks cannot come quickly enough. Around 77% of Mongolia’s land is degraded, and the country is warming three times faster than the global average. Kiers says that paying more attention to fungal networks could help to address the interconnected global challenges of desertification, biodiversity loss and climate change.

It seems that fungi might be starting to get the attention they deserve: last month, at the latest meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, held in Yerevan, Armenia, 3 more countries signed a pledge to conserve fungi, bringing the total number of signatories to 17. And a road map to help countries make good on that pledge, the Global Strategy for Fungal Conservation, was launched.

Kiers’s team is part of the Society for the Protection of Underground Networks (SPUN), a non-profit organization that maps fungal systems around the world and works to protect them. Kiers co-founded the organization in 2021. In September, its researchers announced that they had found more than 500 types of fungus in southwestern Mongolia, 90% of which were previously unknown.

Kiers’s team is in talks with several governments to present its maps of fungal hotspots and data in hopes of supporting the development of strategies to curb desertification and boost climate resilience.

But at the same time as researchers such as Kiers are documenting fungal hotspots, the hotspots might be disappearing. In Mongolia, the team found that degraded land had at least 44% fewer species of mycorrhizal fungi and 60% less plant cover than did non-degraded land.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03589-9

#965. Darts has a new jester with Morris set to light up Grand Slam in Wolverhampton

Remember the name! Tommy Morris became only the sixth non-Tour Card holder to win a ProTour title, and now he is ready to let loose his dance moves at the Grand Slam of Darts; you can watch the tournament in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports from November 14-22

Sports Journalist @RazMirza

Gardener by day, darting superstar by night, Tommy 'The Gun' Morris is ready to rake in his newfound celebrity status when he makes his debut at the Grand Slam of Darts.

Morris, from Dorset, goes by the moniker 'The Gun' - like real-life boxer Tommy Morrison, who co-starred alongside Sylvester Stallone in the 1990 film Rocky V as the Oklahoma boxer Tommy Gunn.

Both have something to prove! The 34-year-old has charisma, style, and some serious dance moves, and now he's set to leave Dimitri van den Bergh, Ricky Evans and Devon Petersen trailing in his shadow.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Morris has already made his mark by beating his idol Gary Anderson, Michael van Gerwen, Rob Cross and Michael Smith - all former world champions.

"It's just proving to people what I can do. This is not just a pub game for me now," Morris declared to Sky Sports.

"At the start of the year I got invited to the first Pro Tour and it became sort of a domino effect. I'm glad I'm finally getting the results because I've kept going and not giving up. It's going great at the minute. It really is."

Morris, who established himself on the MODUS Super Series, revealed he doesn't want to "burst the balloon" when he makes his grand appearance on the big stage in Wolverhampton.

He has been drawn in Group C alongside former World Cup winner Josh Rock and Dutchman Kevin Doets.

"I can dance, but I want to make it a bit of a surprise," he said. "I've got a party theme tune lined up. You're going to love it. I'll have a little shake, and we can have a good vibe. That's what dancing is about - just entertaining!

"I'm a bit of a jester. I'm the fun one in the room. I don't take things as seriously because that one game can make you give up. I want to keep going. I've learned that I need good energy around me.

"This is what is helping me progress. Good people, good vibes. And I'm looking forward to my walk-ons."

Morris officially qualified for the World Championship for the first time, finishing third in the PDC Challenge Tour, but he will also feature at the Players Championship Finals in Minehead, as well as in Wolverhampton.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tournaments are coming thick and fast for Morris, who said: "I'm just going to take it in my stride. If it doesn't go well, I'm still very proud of what I've done, what I'm doing. This is not the end of me. This is a start. So, this is the new progression that I need to get used to the cameras, the bigger stages.

"I'm hoping this develops me better as a player. And if it doesn't, I'm still going to keep working at it, plugging away. But as of today, I'm very proud of what I've done and what I've achieved from the start of the year."

Morris, who suffers from tinnitus in his ear, made it to Players Championship 32 final in Den Bosch where he was beaten by Chris Dobey, but he kept believing in his ability and sealed the Players Championship 34 title in Leicester with an emotional victory over former world champion Luke Humphries - sealed via a 161 checkout.

"I got so emotional when I actually done it. And if I'm honest, that hasn't even sunk in. These little platforms and what I'm doing, they're not really hitting me," he admitted.

"I feel like when I've been at the Pro Tour now, I feel like I can compete with these guys all the time. Not just go down the pub and play Barry the Butcher."

"I do class myself at the minute as one of the best players on the planet right now."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Morris' dream is beyond winning the Wimborne Championship where he resides, but to claim a full-time tour card on the PDC circuit.

He has struck up an unlikely friendship with veteran player Mervyn King, whom he sees as his mentor.

"Merv is one of my best friends in darts right now. If not my best friend, he mentors me. He also calms me down because I'm really fiery and he's really mellow. So this is why we work.

"We don't get into going out to pubs, celebrating. We'll go back, put the TV on and watch Vera or Silent Witness. We're a bit boring.

"We've got fishing trips planned so we're into the same hobbies, which is a bonus for what we do on and off the oche."

Everton have launched a shock bid for former Manchester City man, Kevin De Bruyne.

The Belgian is a legend of the Premier League, having won six titles and racked up an in while racking up almost 200 goal involvements in 288 appearances in the English top flight – but since leaving the Etihad, things haven't been as rosy for him in Italian football.

Now, Everton are prepared to offer the 35-year-old a return to the northwest of England in one of the biggest-name moves of the Toffees' recent history.

De Bruyne spent 10 years at Manchester City before swapping one blue shirt for another and signing for Napoli last summer.

The playmaker has struggled to make a difference in Serie A, however, with Calciomercato reporting that he “appears to be in a decline mentally and could sensationally return to the Premier League in January.”

The report notes that Everton are making a sensational swoop to bring De Bruyne back to England and have already made contact with the player's entourage.

The Merseysiders are up to sixth in the Premier League at the moment and enjoying a good season, despite leaving themselves short over the summer in terms of transfer business.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Fans were disappointed when the club sold striker Beto without a replacement – leaving Thierno Barry as the only recognised No.9 at the Hill Dickinson Stadium – while a failure to replace long-serving right-back Seamus Coleman after his retirement has meant that midfielder Merlin Rohl has taken the role on this term.

There has been recent uncertainty regarding the loan spell of Jack Grealish, too, with the England international dropped by manager David Moyes after breaching the club's disciplinary rules when he reportedly skipped training.

Grealish – who is on loan from Man City, incidentally – has very little chance of joining the Toffees permanently now, with some suggesting that his loan spell could be curtailed in January.

De Bruyne's contract runs until 2027, with the Partenopei holding an option for another year.

Whether club president Aurelio De Laurentiis decides to release the player midseason remains another matter.

The 35-year-old is worth €8 million, as per Transfermarkt. Everton travel away to Brentford when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

Forget the notion of glorified friendlies, this month quarter-final berths, relegation peril, and major tournament seeding is all on the line in the UEFA Nations League.

The final round of group fixtures is anything but an international break distraction.

Here, we break down what it all means for the home nations.

The top two finishers in each League A group advance to a two-legged quarter-final stage, rather than just the group winners qualifying directly for a final-four tournament, as has previously been the case.

This week’s fixtures decide which nations book their place in the knockout bracket to compete for the trophy, while also dictating important top-seed status for the subsequent knockout draw.

The margins between tiers carry significant weight. Finishing top of the group in Leagues B, C, and D earns automatic promotion to the tier above, while finishing bottom of Leagues A, B, and C results in automatic relegation.

Crucially, the introduction of two-legged promotion/relegation play-offs - which will pit third-placed teams in League A against runners-up from League B, and third-placed teams in League B against runners-up from League C - means almost every matchday result directly determines either immediate survival, a climb up the ladder, or a drop into lower-tier fixtures.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Nations League standings double as an insurance policy for future European Championship and FIFA World Cup cycles.

Overall tournament rankings determine the seeding pots for upcoming European qualifying draws, directly affecting the difficulty of qualification paths. The highest-ranked Nations League group winners who fail to secure qualification through standard qualifying groups are handed secondary lifelines via tournament play-off berths.

England currently sit second in their group with nine points, trailing Spain (12 points) but comfortably ahead of Croatia (3 points) and Czechia (0 points).

Because the top two teams in League A advance, Thomas Tuchel's side have already effectively secured their quarter-final berth. The focus now shifts to whether they can overtake Spain for the group's top seed.

Thursday, Nov 12: vs Croatia (H – Wembley Stadium, London) - 19:45 GMT

Sunday, Nov 15: vs Spain (A – Metropolitano Stadium, Madrid) - 19:45 GMT

Wales are third in their top-tier group, trailing Portugal and Denmark, but sitting just above Norway. To avoid a relegation play-off against a League B runner-up or automatic relegation if they drop to fourth, they need results this week to either secure their safety or mount a late push into the top two for a quarter-final spot.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Norway (A – Ullevaal Stadium, Oslo) - 17:00 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Portugal (H – Cardiff City Stadium, Cardiff) - 19:45 GMT

Scotland find themselves in third place behind Switzerland and Slovenia, with North Macedonia rooted to the bottom. Finishing third in League B leads to a relegation play-off against a League C side, so the Tartan Army will be keen to pick up points and push for second place (promotion play-off) or even top spot (automatic promotion).

Friday, Nov 13: vs North Macedonia (H – Hampden Park, Glasgow) - 19:45 GMT

Monday, Nov 16: vs Switzerland (A – Kybunpark, St. Gallen) - 19:45 GMT

Michael O'Neill's side are in an excellent position, currently top of their group ahead of Hungary, Ukraine, and Georgia. If they maintain their first-place standing over the next two games, they will earn automatic promotion to League A.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Ukraine (H – Windsor Park, Belfast) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Hungary (A – Puskas Arena, Budapest) - 19:45 GMT

The Republic of Ireland sit in third on five points, trailing group leaders Austria and second-placed Kosovo. They will need strong performances in this window to climb into the top two for a shot at promotion, or risk facing a relegation play-off to retain their League B status.

Saturday, Nov 14: vs Austria (A – Raiffeisen Arena, Linz) - 19:45 GMT

Tuesday, Nov 17: vs Kosovo (H – Aviva Stadium, Dublin) - 19:45 GMT

Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. #959. Kane’s Ballon d’Or triumph a glorious riposte to celebrity fawning of ceremony | Barney Ronay

The England captain spoke movingly on a night of deserving winners and unintentional hilarity in London

Well, there’s something new. Football: now available in new, genuinely heartwarming flavour.

There was a lovely moment at London’s Palladium theatre on Monday, with the clock creeping towards 11pm at the end of a startlingly shrill and bloated evening of never‑ending awards and never-ending award‑related excitement.

Not just for Harry Kane, who is now the 2026 men’s Ballon d’Or winner, and in the process placed indelibly in that lineage of elite footballers. But also, frankly, for anyone watching, as Kane stood on stage gazing a little shyly at his golden orb, and kicked off his speech by thanking everyone, paying tribute to everyone, everywhere, then finally cracking into tears and a strangled croak as he thanked his parents for sacrifices made, his wife for always being there, and even, in slightly jarring vibe-shift from the warm honeyed tone, José Mourinho.

Even Kane’s biggest advocates will rarely claim their man is one of a kind, sui generis, in the mode of the Ronaldo-Messi godhead. But Kane is exactly this in his own admirably humble way.

Not just an exceptional footballer, the best, most deserving men’s player in the world this year, a European golden boot, scorer of 89 goals since August 2025, Bundesliga champion, World Cup semi-final captain, model of extreme professionalism and care. He’s also quite clearly the nicest man, if not just in football, then possibly the world.

Or at least it felt like that as he walked off in that very dear and tender way, the centre of the world in that moment, but also just keen to get off the stage and let everyone get on with clearing up.

It would be wrong to say Kane’s victory in the final vote of the night redeemed the grotesqueness of the ceremonies itself. There was a roomful of hugely deserving winners here. But Kane hits particularly hard.

And the Ballon d’Or is, let us be clear, a horrendous event, albeit a supremely popular horrendous event. There was the usual pomp around the ceremony, staged this year at a fancy theatre close to Oxford Circus.

This isn’t sport. It’s celebrity culture, red‑carpet fawning, the worship of images and people, and fame. Football isn’t supposed to be cocooned this way, to send the message that there are barriers and ropes and special people. Yeah, well, good luck with that.

The night kicked off with French Montana in spotless white tuxedo performing on an open-air double-decker bus. He definitely speaks, clearly, carried well, seemed enthusiastic. If it all goes south from here, the evidence suggests French Montana could, at the very least, get a job as a London tour bus operator.

Before long Thierry Henry and Kate Scott glided on stage, half an hour late, to add a little deft and easy charm to a furious schedule of pots and prizes.

And the awards came thick and fast. The Spain manager, Luis de la Fuente, was named coach of the year. “I hope in the future I will become in English better,” were his first words at the lectern, throwing his hat in the ring for a disastrous pension-padding six months at Manchester United two years from now.

There was a lovely moment as Burna Boy came on to present the Socrates award for charitable works to Bukayo Saka. He was asked if there were footballers who had inspired his love for the game. At which point he looked at Thierry and said, “definitely, one of them’s standing right there”, and of course he said it in his Burna Boy voice, looking Thierry deep in the eyes so smooth and deep, just almost an impossibly sexy moment.

The Ballon d’Or can be unintentionally hilarious at times such as these. There were just so, so many video tributes, so much excitingly portentous music. This is a stage where everyone happening at every moment is very clearly the most important thing ever to happen, superseded only by the next thing to happen on that stage, and then the thing after that.

The degree of fawning is startling at first, but glazed by familiarity before long. At one point Cristiano Ronaldo appeared very briefly in a fact-cut big-screen montage and the crowd shrieked a song, clutched its hand to its fevered throat, collapsed into the aisles in sheer priapic excitement.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Although by the time the original Ronaldo emerged onstage at 10.44pm, there was a sense of the genuinely vertiginous company Kane was about to join. Ronaldo read out the name inside the envelope, and the hall collapsed into cheers and yells and roars as Kane appeared onstage.

And yes the Ballon d’Or is a fundamentally silly thing on its own terms. It jars with the basic concept of team sport, promoting instead the opposite of sport, the opposite of team culture, the modern disease of fawning parasocial engagement with star names. In many ways the world would be a better place if the Ballon d’Or was simply abolished, as an example to all who pore over reels and clips and the imagined qualities of their celebrity paramours.

But it is also fascinating, unignorable, and endlessly moreish. All the more so this time. Kane as the Ballon d’Or 2026 is a genuinely fine, uplifting, instructive moment in the spotlight.

It is always tempting to talk about the journey these players make. Everyone has a backstory. Most footballers come from adversity. Kane has this, in his own way, 16 years into a professional career which has names such as Leyton Orient, Millwall, Leicester and Norwich on the timelines. He was unexceptional as a junior, didn’t stand out as particularly skilful or big or outstanding in his numbers. He played as a holding midfielder for a bit while Spurs decided what to do with him.

Kane worked relentlessly. He was Millwall young player of the year in 2012, fitting bookend to the Ballon. He made it because he simply refused to go away, to stop working, honed instead the deeper skills in his quiver, the purity of his shooting, the range of his passing long and short.

And Kane is exceptional in other ways. Without ever peacocking around promoting his brand, without really trying he remains the most likable, authentic, role‑model‑ish modern-day England player. For a man who never talks big or acts big he has a happy knack of becoming the key player wherever he goes. Perhaps Kane has become cool now. He has always been likable, with that mild-mannered air of a kindly Victorian chimney sweep with a hamster in his waistcoat watch pocket. In the Bayern years, Kane has become leaner, more glossed and handsome, jawline, tan, iconic Vampire hairline.

Mainly he expresses a common confusion about what talent really is. Talent isn’t simply moments. Talent is also application, focus, craft, the ability to work, to make others better.

And yet his elite career has also been oddly grudging. Somehow the idea has always been out there that Kane is undeserving of these accolades, despite his own mildness and humility, his obvious team qualities, his relentless delivery of goals, effort, leadership. It is a genuinely odd conclusion given the opposite is so manifestly true, that this is an entirely uplifting story of overachievement, of hard work and applied intelligence, as opposed to the kind of talent that just needs to be flame‑throwered in the right direction.

It is undeniably true that Kane’s levels can drop dramatically when he can’t perform at his full physical capacity. There have been moments where it has been tempting to wonder if he’s gone far enough as England’s captain in the past few years, if his body and his talent deserve a little care.

Well, that just shows how wrong you can be.

England crashed out of the World Cup in what felt like a tactical collapse - and the Three Lions' biggest names have been painfully honest about the exit

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

England players aired “strong views” in the wake of the World Cup 2026 collapse at the hands of Argentina.

That's according to a report that states says that arguably the Three Lions' two best players, Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham, have been particularly strong in expressing their opinions over the defeat.

With plenty blaming manager Thomas Tuchel for negative tactics, “All players were afforded an opportunity to air their personal views during the meeting”, with “some of the squad” holding “grievances” after the game.

England were in a strong position to make their first World Cup final in 60 years when they came up against an Argentina side in Atlanta that had been dragged to the final four by Lionel Messi.

Despite the struggles of the reigning champions, however, the Albiceleste managed to get the job done late in the semi, overturning Anthony Gordon's opening strike to set up a showpiece against Spain in New Jersey – which they in turn lost.

According to the BBC's Sami Mokbel, a September meeting allowed for the squad to express how they felt about the collapse, which was blamed on Tuchel sitting back to protect the slender advantage against the brilliance of Messi.

As noted, “a number of senior England players held misgivings at Tuchel's instructions for the closing stages of the Argentina loss, believing the approach was too negative and defensive,” with “captain Harry Kane… strong and forthright with his views.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Bellingham was mentioned by name, too, as being “particularly candid” in expressing that he felt his side were superior man-for-man to the opposition.

Mokbel continues to mention that Bellingham's contribution in the meeting has “underlined his growing influence” with his national team, as many believe he could assume the captain's armband from Harry Kane, once the Ballon d'Or winner retires from international duty.

Real Madrid midfielder Bellingham re-established himself as one of his country's most important players in North America over the summer, despite heading into the tournament with question marks over how much of a role he would play under Tuchel.

The 23-year-old was in and out of the German's plans during qualification, with Morgan Rogers preferred at times in the No.10 role.

Bellingham has played 60 times for his country and scored 14 times. England host Croatia this Thursday night.

The Manchester United hierarchy must not disregard relegation as an impossibility after one win in their opening 10 league matches this season

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada and technical director Jason Wilcox are scheduled to sit down with Sir Jim Ratcliffe in Monaco this week.

Head coach Michael Carrick’s future is expected to dominate the agenda at the pre-planned meeting in the principality where Ratcliffe is based. There is every chance a far more unpalatable subject will also be confronted given Man United's start to the 2026/27 season: drafting a contingency plan for relegation.

Ten games into the Premier League campaign, Man United find themselves in the bottom three with just a solitary victory. Minority owners INEOS arrived at Old Trafford boasting elite operating standards and a clear structure but on the pitch, the team has been dragged into a survival scrap for the second year running.

Acknowledging the drop remains something of a taboo for a club of Man United's size and commercial footprint, but a recent warning from north London shows why ignoring it would constitute negligence.

Speaking on The Sports Agents podcast, Tottenham Hotspur chief executive Vinai Venkatesham revealed how the club were planning for the future after Spurs flirted with disaster last season.

“It's really tough, because you form a relationship with people. Obviously, Igor [Tudor] wasn't the coach for long, but Thomas [Frank], we worked together really, really, really closely, went through some really difficult times," Venkatesham explained.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Spurs ultimately secured survival on the final day, but Venkatesham admitted the club had quietly mapped out a blueprint for the Championship.

“It was really challenging. A really, really, really challenging period for the club,” he said. “You have to [prepare for relegation]. I mean, you can't not. To not make that plan would have been irresponsible… Sometimes going through something as traumatic as what we went through last season bonds people a little bit and also puts even more fire in everybody's belly to make sure that something like that can never happen again.”

That brush with the drop motivated Spurs to spend £300 million on summer transfer targets, including £100m on Newcastle United's Sandro Tonali and £85m on West Ham United midfielder Matheus Fernandes.

“Everybody was aligned we wanted to strengthen this position, and then everybody was aligned that Matheus [Fernandes] was absolutely the number one target,” Venkatesham said. “If I'm honest, we achieved more than we thought we might do, and that was really because so many of our number one targets we were able to land. Because if we weren't going to get our number one targets, we weren't going to settle.”

Even with morale lifted by recent wins, Venkatesham reflected honestly on their sluggish start: “I wasn't worried [by the start to the 2026/27 season], but I was definitely frustrated… Did we think we were going to make this many changes and everything would gel straight away? Of course we didn't. But did we think we'd be hovering around the position of the league that we were in the international break? Of course we didn't either.”

For Ratcliffe, Berrada, and Wilcox, Venkatesham’s transparency should rid them of any lingering delusions of grandeur. Precedent proves that stature, revenue, and history offer little insulation once a club slips into the bottom three.

Whether Man United decide to back Carrick through the November break or sack him, the decision-making trio at the Monaco summit cannot afford to treat the drop as an unthinkable scenario.

That might mean re-thinking squad wage-reduction clauses or auditing broadcast revenue drop-offs, because after all, responsible governance demands preparing for the worst.

If Man United pretend they are simply too big to go down, that is the quickest way to end up there.

Joe joined FourFourTwo as senior digital writer in July 2025 after five years covering Leeds United in the Championship and Premier League. Joe's 'Mastermind' specialist subject is 2000s-era Newcastle United having had a season ticket at St. James' Park for 10 years before relocating to Leeds and later London. Joe takes a keen interest in youth football, covering PL2, U21 Euros, as well as U20 and U17 World Cups in the past, in addition to hosting the industry-leading football recruitment-focused SCOUTED podcast. He is also one of the lucky few to have 'hit top bins' as a contestant on Soccer AM. It wasn't a shin-roller.

#955. A phone-free Yellow Wall: are Dortmund urging fans to be present or policing them?

It makes sense that sports teams want to keep influencers out of their games. The battle some clubs are waging with their fans, however, is a different dilemma

By all appearances, things on the Yellow Wall seemed as they always had been. The stadium announcer hollered out the first names of Borussia Dortmund’s starting lineup and the supporters responded with their last names, tens of thousands of voices bellowing as one. Dozens of black and yellow flags waved over Europe’s largest standing terrace, a mass of faces fixed on the field beneath them.

And then Signal Iduna Park, sold out with 81,365 fans, roared when Max Beier’s lone goal led Dortmund to victory over Eintracht Frankfurt last Saturday, putting the home side even on points with Bayern Munich atop the Bundesliga standings.

Yet, apparently, a crisis of a sort has been churning just below the surface of what is, by broad consensus, Europe’s best home support.

On Friday, Dortmund had announced a kind of bribery scheme. A rewards program is probably a kinder way of putting it. Fans who stayed off their phones during the bout with Eintracht had the chance to win signed jerseys and earn gift cards to the club’s merchandise store. If they activated a so-called “fan mode” on the club’s app – a name so phenomenally passive-aggressive you can only applaud whoever came up with it – the club could count who unlocked their phones the fewest times during the game. For every minute the fans left their phones alone, they got points.

Dortmund are not the only German team to pick a fight with phones.

Second-division clubs Hertha Berlin and Dynamo Dresden have banned commercial influencer-style videos in their stadiums altogether, fearing for both the integrity of the TV rights they sell and the experience of their fans. Dortmund, likewise, appear motivated by the incursion of influencers, who are siphoning off and monetizing footage of the famous match-day experience and growing into a nuisance for regulars.

This problem has also afflicted the tennis majors. The US Open now resembles an influencer convention more than it does a tennis tournament. When the US Tennis Association credentialed more than 100 content creators this year, the influencers grew so disruptive that a match was stopped when a chair umpire had to ask them to turn off a ring light. Wimbledon has refused to credential influencers for just this reason, which doesn’t stop them from getting in with regular tickets or through sponsors.

Dortmund’s attempt at shaping fan behavior, however, goes further than warding off the cultural content parasites. This please-stop-holding-up-your-phones-and-just-live-in-the-present plea raises quasi-existential questions about sport and its consumption.

“Over 81,000 people in the stadium, singing, cheering, and holding their breath together: this here and now is irreplaceable,” Dortmund chief executive Carsten Cramer said. “And that’s exactly what we’re putting front and center together.”

“Anyone at a soccer game should experience the moment and the emotions – not just a cell phone screen,” added Marcel de Groot, the chief executive of Vodafone Germany, both a cellphone service provider and a Dortmund sponsor. “Let’s leave our smartphones in our pockets more often at the stadium and instead focus on what’s happening on the field and in the stands.”

These were statements delivered with unshakeable confidence in their righteousness, yet there is evidence to suggest this simply isn’t how some fans want to behave at stadiums.

Which begs the question: can, and should, professional sports teams get to dictate how their ticket-buying fans experience their games? It’s surely a question that’s crossed the mind of all the musicians who now perform to a sea of cell phones, their flashlights on, obscuring the faces in the crowd. Did their fans buy the right to experience the concert as they please? Or does this objectify the musicians and diminish the performance, somehow?

It goes back to the question of whether sport is entertainment, and whether its consumers get to sit back and let the proceedings and the attendant stimuli wash over them. Or whether they are something else entirely: active participants in the games they attend. If that is so, then fandom amounts to a parasocial relationship conferring membership to a community with attendant behavioral expectations.

What are the responsibilities of the ticketholder? Do teams get to purity-test their supporters? What do fans owe their teams? Is live soccer just content? A day out, not unlike going to the movies or a museum, where nobody expects total focus and for you to cheer on the thing you’re looking at? Is it heresy to even suggest this?

The latter tends to be the view, or at least the vibe, in most American sports leagues where fans are often less engaged, told by an announcer and a jumbo screen when and what to clap or stomp or chant. This has always contrasted with the feel of global football, where the folklore is usually organic, sparked and dictated by the fans themselves. It’s why all of those pre-game and half-time concerts at the World Cup final rankled, drowning out the thrum of the throaty Argentina fans.

It feels both instructive and fitting that this debate broke out at Dortmund. The Bundesliga’s rules on safeguarding fan majority ownership of very nearly every club have preserved the league as a kind of supporters’ paradise, with relatively cheap tickets and policies that put fans first. Dortmund, for their part, have been held up for years as a paradigm for their following – thus attracting the influencers, of course.

The latter will be dealt with, it seems. In an age when soccer clubs are essentially production houses who also field company teams, it always seemed inevitable that these interlopers would be expelled from the premises. The fans, however, are not so easily corrected on behavior their teams have deemed undesirable. And they will vote with their credit cards.

Leander Schaerlaeckens is the author of The Long Game: U.S. Men’s Soccer and Its Savage, Four-Decade Journey to the Top, or Thereabouts, which is out now. He teaches at Marist University.

Arsenal are set to lose a major first-teamer in the January transfer market

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Arsenal are on the cusp of losing a major star this January.

The Gunners enjoyed a solid if not spectacular summer transfer window, bringing in Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa and Christos Tzolis to add quality and depth to a title-winning side.

But with competition fierce for places, it appears that one Arsenal player is set to leave to seek game time elsewhere.

Mikel Arteta's side are top of the Premier League table, five points clear, unbeaten in the Champions League, and have only lost twice in all competitions this season.

But not everyone is happy with their role in N5, and now, RNE Deportes originally broke the news of a departure, with further updated relayed in a report by Sport Witness.

Martin Zubimendi is on the cusp of leaving for Atletico Madrid, as per Relevo, with his relationship with Arteta said to be “cold”, following “friction towards the end of last season”.

Another Spanish outlet, AS, adds that Arsenal need to sell, and would like to recoup the £50 million they spent on the Basque midfielder.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Zubimendi only moved to the Emirates Stadium in 2025, with the Gunners beating a host of rivals for his signature after a star turn in the Euro 2024 final.

The 27-year-old became an instant hit alongside Declan Rice in Arteta's engine room, providing the progression and anticipation that the side had missed in that area of the pitch, becoming almost ever-present in the first half of Arsenal's title-winning season.

But as the season neared the run-in, Zubimendi found himself dropped in favour of Hale Ender, Myles Lewis-Skelly, and didn't start the Champions League final – with Arsenal upgrading in the summer to sign Bruno Guimaraes.

Zubimendi has not started a single league game in midfield for Arsenal this term, finding himself fourth in the pecking order in midfield.

FourFourTwo understands that Arsenal would rather not sell the World Cup winner this January and would prefer to wait until the summer to assess the situation further.

Zubimendi is worth €65m, according to Transfermarkt. Arsenal travel away to Newcastle United when Premier League action resumes after the international break.

#952. 'A beautiful story' as Bellingham brothers called up

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could be the first brothers to play together for England since Gary and Phil Neville 19 years ago

It may be a surprise to some but Jobe Bellingham's call-up to the England senior side has been a long time coming.

The 21-year-old's career path has been very similar to that of his 23-year-old brother Jude - England's star player at the World Cup and one of Real Madrid's best players. Both were stars of the Birmingham City academy before big-money moves to the German Bundesliga and England call-ups.

Jobe's debut for Birmingham came at the age of 16 years and 107 days - 69 days older than Jude when he made his first appearance for the Blues' senior side.

The central midfielder then moved to Sunderland and helped them win promotion to the Premier League before joining German side Borussia Dortmund at the age of 19 in a deal worth up to Â£31m.

Jude also moved to Dortmund when he was 17, before developing into one of the world's best players and joining Real Madrid.

Having one of the best midfielders in the world as your older brother comes with challenges and Jobe has consistently been compared to his sibling.

But the former Sunderland midfielder is his own player, wearing 'Jobe' on the back of his shirt instead of his family name. He said it was suggested to him by a former coach because "it shows that I'm going my own way".

England manager Thomas Tuchel told BBC Radio 5 Live it is "a beautiful story".

"They are both good for each other," he added. "My understanding is they are very close.

"It makes life easier for Jobe to come into camp and know his brother is one of the key players in our team. So, that will hopefully help him, but don't forget he is here on his own merits, and he is not here because of his brother."

Jobe is a different type of player to Jude, sitting deeper in the midfield, but is as physically imposing while still being good on the ball.

He is the current captain of the England Under-21 side, and Tuchel said Young Lions head coach Lee Carsley had been pushing for some time for the younger Bellingham to get senior recognition.

"He's the standout player," said Tuchel. "He's the captain, so the door should always be open for the pathway, always be open for special performances over a long period of time.

"That's what Jobe has done on top of it. He found his way, he found his rhythm with Dortmund. He's had an excellent start to his season, is a regular starter and influential."

Thomas Tuchel on Jobe Bellingham's England call-up

England host Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November before travelling to Madrid to take on Spain on 15 November in this next international break.

With Arsenal's Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended for the first game, and Bournemouth's Alex Scott out injured after shining on his debut in last month's 7-0 win over Croatia, Tuchel said a natural "opportunity" for Jobe had opened up.

"He deserves to make an impression for us," said the German in his news conference after naming the squad.

"It's an incredible achievement for the family and for the brothers. I saw his excitement straight away and his smile.

"He has an open and calm personality. He's one of five players for the central midfield.

"He's a more defensive player than Jude. So strong on the ball, good physique, a big body, a very physical player and can keep possession.

"It's now up to him, but he's excited and happy and eager to impress, and that's the best foundation to have a good camp for him."

Jude shared a throwback photo of him and Jobe after Friday's squad announcement

If they get on the pitch together, Jude and Jobe won't be the first brothers to represent the Three Lions.

It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville, who both played for Manchester United, last played together for England, and 30 years since they started.

They first played together for England in 1996 against China, becoming the first siblings to do so since Bobby and Jack Charlton 26 years earlier.

Jack and Bobby were both part of England's 1966 World Cup-winning squad.

Bobby was the younger of the two, but made his Three Lions debut first. He went on to win 106 international caps.

Jack, who was not called into the England team until days before his 30th birthday, won 35 caps.

More recently, brothers Nathaniel and Trevoh Chalobah have both played for England, but never alongside each other.

Nathaniel made his solitary appearance as an injury-time substitute in a 3-2 away win against Spain in a 2018 Nations League game.

His younger brother Trevoh, currently a Como defender, made the first of his three international appearances against Senegal in June 2025 and was in England's 2026 World Cup squad.

Bobby and Jack Charlton were both in the England squad that lifted the Jules Rimet Trophy at Wembley.

The Chalobah brothers never played together for England, but both featured for the senior side.

Jobe Bellingham has made 14 appearances for Dortmund this season

Jobe has shown remarkable progress since last winter. In the first couple of months, following his move from Sunderland to Borussia Dortmund, he seemed timid, as if he was just trying to avoid making any mistakes. His passes rarely, if ever, caused trouble for opposing defences.

Even Dortmund manager Niko Kovac said at one point that he was surprised how long it might take him to get comfortable in the Bundesliga. But hard work in the gym to build up muscle mass in order to become more explosive and the fact that he received plenty of chances in Dortmund's line-up has helped his development.

In the latter stages of last season, his decision-making was much faster and his intensity seemed higher. Still, Dortmund decided to sign Dutch midfielder Joey Veerman, a specialist at making line-breaking passes, in August.

It meant Jobe's place in the starting XI was far from secure at the beginning of this season.

In recent games, Kovac has employed Bellingham in a more advanced role, as one of the two number 10s behind the striker. In this role, Bellingham drove into the final third with pace and showed intensity during pressing sequences.

His performance in the 2-2 draw against Bayern Munich in the Bundesliga last Saturday was arguably his best since his arrival in Germany.

#951. How can playing for Manchester City fit into Marc Guéhi’s moral universe? | Barney Ronay

Club’s predicament raises interesting questions about principles, both for individuals and the Premier League

I felt unbelievably ponderous. My head was made of Aztec stone. I realised I didn’t want to be with all these people. Somebody came at me, a huge individual in silver and blue. I fell at his feet and grabbed one shoe. I started untying the lace. He kicked away from me. I got up and walked off. I was exceedingly hungry.

Not my words. Also not the words of the Manchester City centre-back Marc Guéhi, despite what you were thinking there. This is instead a condensed quote from the mind of Gary Harkness, existentially curious college running-back and the narrator of Don DeLillo’s great American football novel End Zone.

This passage describes a moment where Gary plays a game having been urged by his friends to smoke pot beforehand to discover whether it improves his understanding of time and space, or just makes him want to lie down and untie someone’s laces. It marks a turning point for Gary. To this point football has been a comforting world. He sees clarity in its militaristic rituals, finds in sport “the illusion that order is possible”, hears hidden truths in the coaches’ shouted instructions. Button up. Get fetal. Get fetal. Get fetal. Run with reckless abandon.

Now the illusion has collapsed. Gary walks off the football field and begins instead to fixate on cold war fears and nuclear apocalypse. Death and political power have entered the chat.

Now, I’m not saying Marc Guéhi is Gary Harkness. You might be saying that. That’s your choice. But Guéhi has seemed a bit distracted in the last few weeks. Oddly for an agile and technically sound centre-back, he has seemed brittle and absent, vulnerable to being pressed.

There have been a couple of things said about City’s players in this regard. The first is that their minds might not be wholly on the game, that in the middle of a game against Croatia, for example, concerned only with manoeuvring through tiny pockets of space, Nico O’Reilly is also thinking: “Hmm, but how is it possible even by omission to honestly contravene rules E.3 and E.4 which state clearly that …oh. Wait, no. Oh dear.”

Football doesn’t work like this. The physical game is a place of total focus. But still, nothing is watertight. And this speaks to the second thing people have said, repeated like an absolute truth, that the players are entirely separate from all this. They cannot be questioned here, or indeed expected to ask questions of their own. The players are simply avatars, employees, free from any kind of agency. Players don’t have access to Google. They cannot make moral judgments. And yes, this may not be true of any other human in any other field. It may be the case that elite footballers are in fact unusually empowered, free to do whatever they want. But the consensus is clear. It is not a footballer’s business to have opinions on their employers, or what happens out of their line of vision.

This does help to avoid some tricky conundrums. Guéhi, for example, is a man of absolute public principle. Fair enough. I respect his willingness to resist popular pressure and personalise his support for the rainbow armband by writing things about Jesus on top of it. This is living your values. It’s free speech, figuring out your own moral universe. Doing so by following the absolute tenets of his religion. Go for it.

At the same time, Guéhi is playing for a club that has been convicted of cheating and lying. People are free to disagree with the rules. But if others are sticking to them, this amounts to deceit, stolen win bonuses, stolen glory. And the Bible is very clear on this. Thessalonians 4:6: “No one should transgress and defraud his brother.” Proverbs 20:17: “Bread gained by deceit is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be full of gravel.” Now, I don’t believe these words to be divinely ordained. They’re great words. Totally dig the vibe. But Guéhi does believe these things to be an absolute instruction. How does this fit together in his head? How does that gravel (pending appeal) taste right now?

Again, fine if you can square it. It’s a personal journey. Park the apparent moral dilemma. See if your legal team can come up with a better final outcome. But things have changed in one significant way since the verdict dropped, an element that is now unchallenged, and which has been largely unremarked in the middle of the chaos. Understandably so. This stuff is gruelling. Everyone just wants to watch some football in the brief lull between legal rage events. But there are two points worth making in the interim. The second of which is an admission that affects many other things.

The first issue is: do you actually understand the basis of the Manchester City appeal? That evidence has seemingly been leaked. The irrefutable body of evidence, Body Of Evidence 2, the long-awaited tribunal-based Madonna erotic thriller vehicle, contains a vital detail: the additional money in City’s coffers, almost a billion, did not come from the owners, the Abu Dhabi United Group, which is owned, like City, by Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan. This would be against the rules. It came instead from the Abu Dhabi government, which is essentially the Abu Dhabi royal family, of which Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan is a member; as he is also, wearing a different hat, of the Abu Dhabi government.

And maybe this means it’s fine. It seems the government often tops up the sponsor companies like a benevolent uncle. In the period the charges relate to there was no need for sponsor deals to be of market value, as there is now. So if we accept all this, if we can establish a binding principle of wearing different hats in different rooms, this may be a way out. Maybe.

This is a familiar concept in the high court, in an age of shell companies and tricky fiscal flows. Mega-million cases hang on whether ownership really is separate, or whether this is, to echo a phrase, a sham process. The person on the Clapham omnibus might not buy any of this. Do these really seem like separate entities? Or a bit like adopting a French accent when the bailiffs ring up and maintaining that, no, Monsieur Ronay is not here, and he definitely doesn’t run this dry cleaners. That, instead, is me.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

If you make the case you win the case. This is all in the end about the application of rules, and that is a good thing. But the key point here is the secondary issue derived from this. City’s leaked defence, in making their case, is also saying, without pretence or mucking about, that the club is indeed funded by the Abu Dhabi government. This is something City’s fans have at times weirdly denied. But we have it in plain sight now, not just admitted but insisted on. The ultimate source of the dizzying success of the club that has defined a Premier League era is the government. Guéhi is, in effect, an Abu Dhabi civil servant. Perhaps the United Arab Emirates national team should have six stars on their jersey, one for each Premier League won. But there is no way of covering your ears now. City actively want us to accept this.

What are the consequences of this new fact? It comes with two urgent questions. The first is the moral one. Back again to Guéhi as the best example. This is what he is promoting here. And Guéhi is a man entirely guided by the principles of his faith. A private matter perhaps, except that it’s not, because Guéhi’s church explicitly orders its members to go out and proselytise. Guéhi is a member of Ballers in God, which actively tries to awaken Christian faith in the dressing room. He plays with Christian messages on his matchday kit intended to make you, the reader, think yes, maybe I too should follow this evangelical church.

And here is the key thing. This is a criminal offence in Abu Dhabi. Under UAE penal code, giving out Christian leaflets will get you arrested. A Christian pastor in the UAE was sentenced to a year in prison for giving a Muslim a Bible. Some Americans were deported for giving out Christian literature in the Dubai shopping district. Spreading the gospel, which Guéhi is morally bound to do, is illegal in the place that pays his direct employers.

Are players just avatars, empty shells? How much do you really believe in this? These are, more than ever, very interesting questions. And they don’t just apply to issues of personal principle.

The regulator now has this information, too. Abu Dhabi funded the purchase of Nolito. Abu Dhabi dictated the flow of English football finance. The same pocket that paid for this is also funding at arm’s length the civil war in Sudan, the hospital massacres, the piles of bodies so high they can be seen from satellite imaging. Abu Dhabi, which criminalises homosexuality, which crushes dissent, is openly identifying itself as the mega-funder of a Premier League club. Is this a fit and proper influence?

There are very obvious reasons why this is not desirable. Governments spy and wage war and break rules. They have a sacred trust to promote their own interests by any means necessary. It is hard to see how this kind of owner fits the regulatory framework. Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund had to twirl through semantic hoops when buying Newcastle to establish it was an entity at one remove from a government, as opposed to a government entity. In making the opposite case for their funding City have not only exposed their own live-your-values central defender, they have put themselves in a place where, even if you win on one front, you’ve started to look like a very strange presence.

This deserves to be unravelled in all its wider implications. It may be the biggest issue here, whatever the final verdict. How can this be the right thing? How can City’s fans look their own autocratic government-funded club in the eye? The quiet thing has been said out loud. And its implications are bigger than the game, bigger than legal opinion. Enough, perhaps to make you question the existential point of this thing, where the best course of action really might be to walk off and look for the nearest cheeseburger.
